title: Abstract Syntax Trees
tagline: The tree data structure at the heart of every compiler, linter, formatter, and transpiler — and how to walk it.

sections.content:
Every time you save a TypeScript file and your editor underlines a type error within milliseconds, an **Abstract Syntax Tree** is involved. Every time Prettier reformats your messy code into perfectly aligned prose, it is working with an AST. Every time Babel converts `?.` optional chaining into something that Internet Explorer can run, it traverses an AST, rewrites nodes, and prints the result back as text. The AST is the universal medium through which language tooling understands, judges, and transforms code.

An **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)** is a tree-shaped data structure where every node represents a syntactic construct in the source code — a number literal, a binary operation, a function declaration, an `if` statement, a class definition. The tree is *hierarchical*: the root is the whole program, its children are top-level statements, each statement's children are its constituent sub-expressions, and so on, down to leaf nodes that represent atomic values like `42` or `"hello"`.

The word **abstract** is deliberate and meaningful. It distinguishes an AST from a raw **parse tree** (also called a concrete syntax tree, or CST). A parse tree captures every token the parser saw — parentheses, semicolons, commas, the grammar rule that produced each group. An AST throws all of that surface notation away. Parentheses vanish because their purpose — encoding operator precedence — is now captured by the tree's own depth. Semicolons vanish because they carry no semantic information. What remains is only the structure that determines *what the code means*.

Understanding ASTs puts you at the frontier of language tooling. It means you can write your own ESLint rules, author a Babel transform, build a static analyser, or implement a subset of a scripting language in a weekend. Every compiler course, every language specification, and every major developer tool is ultimately speaking the language of trees. This chapter builds that literacy from scratch: how source text becomes an AST, what the nodes look like in practice, how tools walk and transform the tree, and how to build simple tooling yourself.

sections.title: A Blueprint Versus a Photograph
sections.content:
Imagine you want to analyse the structural integrity of a building. You could work from a photograph — but photographs include irrelevant detail: paint colour, window curtains, shadows, decorative mouldings. None of that affects the load-bearing structure. An **architect's blueprint** strips all of that away, showing only what matters: room dimensions, wall materials, electrical conduit paths, load-bearing columns.

Source code is like the photograph. An **AST is the blueprint**. The photograph (source text) has parentheses for grouping, semicolons as statement terminators, whitespace for human readability, and one-liner if-statements written without braces. The blueprint (AST) has none of that. It has a `BinaryExpression` node whose left child is a `CallExpression` — the tree shape already encodes grouping and precedence without a single parenthesis token.

When ESLint checks your code for violations, or Babel rewrites arrow functions for old browsers, they are working from the blueprint. The photograph is only needed at the very beginning (parsing) and the very end (code generation). In between, it is all trees.

sections.title: The Two Phases Before the AST: Lexing and Parsing
sections.content:
Source code starts as a flat string of characters. Two transformations happen before you get an AST.

**Phase 1 — Lexing (tokenisation).** The lexer (also called scanner) reads the character stream left-to-right and groups characters into **tokens** — the smallest meaningful units of the language. The string `const x = 1 + 2;` becomes the token sequence: `[KEYWORD:const] [IDENT:x] [PUNCT:=] [NUM:1] [PUNCT:+] [NUM:2] [PUNCT:;]`. Each token has a type and a value. Whitespace is typically discarded at this stage (it is not a token; it merely separates tokens). Comments may be preserved as special tokens or discarded depending on whether the toolchain needs them (Prettier, for example, preserves comments).

**Phase 2 — Parsing.** The parser reads the token stream and builds a tree according to the language's **grammar** — the formal rules describing which sequences of tokens are valid and how they nest. Most language grammars are written in a notation called **BNF (Backus-Naur Form)** or **EBNF**. The parser uses these rules to recognise, for example, that `1 + 2` is a `BinaryExpression` with operator `+`, left operand `Literal(1)`, and right operand `Literal(2)`. It builds a **parse tree** that mirrors the grammar rules exactly, then typically simplifies that into an **AST** by collapsing single-child rule nodes and dropping punctuation.

For our purposes, we do not need to implement a lexer or parser from scratch — excellent libraries do this for every popular language. In JavaScript, `acorn` and `@babel/parser` are the most widely used; TypeScript has its own compiler API. What matters is understanding the AST they produce and how to traverse it.

flowchart TD

sections.title: Anatomy of an AST Node
sections.content:
Every node in a JavaScript AST (following the **ESTree specification**, which Babel, ESLint, and acorn all share) is a plain JavaScript object with at least a `type` field. The `type` is a string naming the syntactic construct. Additional fields depend on the type.

Here are the most important node types you will encounter:

**`Literal`** — a constant value in the source. Fields: `value` (the actual JS value), `raw` (the source string as written, e.g. `'42'` vs `42`).

**`Identifier`** — any name: variable names, function names, property names. Field: `name` (the string).

**`BinaryExpression`** — an infix operator expression like `a + b` or `x === y`. Fields: `operator` (the operator symbol string), `left` (left operand node), `right` (right operand node).

**`UnaryExpression`** — a prefix operator like `!flag` or `-x`. Fields: `operator`, `argument`, `prefix` (boolean).

**`CallExpression`** — a function call like `foo(a, b)`. Fields: `callee` (the expression being called — an Identifier for named functions, a MemberExpression for method calls), `arguments` (array of argument nodes).

**`MemberExpression`** — property access like `obj.prop` or `arr[i]`. Fields: `object`, `property`, `computed` (false for dot notation, true for bracket notation).

**`FunctionDeclaration`** — `function name(params) { body }`. Fields: `id` (Identifier), `params` (array), `body` (BlockStatement).

**`ArrowFunctionExpression`** — `(params) => body`. Fields: `params`, `body` (either a BlockStatement or an expression for concise arrows), `expression` (boolean).

**`VariableDeclaration`** — `let`, `const`, or `var` statement. Fields: `declarations` (array of VariableDeclarator), `kind` (`'let'`, `'const'`, or `'var'`).

**`IfStatement`** — `if (test) consequent else alternate`. Fields: `test`, `consequent`, `alternate` (null if no else branch).

**`ReturnStatement`** — `return expr`. Field: `argument` (the returned expression, or null for bare `return`).

Every node also carries **`start`**, **`end`**, and **`loc`** fields — the character offset and line/column position in the original source. These are critical for error messages ("Line 17, column 4: unexpected token") and source maps.

sections.title: How Operator Precedence Lives in Tree Depth
sections.content:
One of the subtlest and most important properties of an AST is how it encodes **operator precedence without parentheses**. Consider the expression `x * 2 + 5`. In text, we rely on the convention that `*` binds tighter than `+` — we know mentally that this means `(x * 2) + 5`, not `x * (2 + 5)`. The parser knows this too because the grammar assigns multiplication a higher precedence level than addition.

In the AST, this knowledge is structurally encoded: the multiplication node is a **child** of the addition node. A child must be fully evaluated before its parent can be evaluated. So the tree structure itself says: evaluate `x * 2` first, then add `5` to the result.

If you wrote `x * (2 + 5)` instead — with explicit parentheses overriding the default precedence — the parentheses would flip which node is the child. The addition would become the child of the multiplication. Parentheses are only needed in the source text to override default precedence; in the AST they are gone because the tree already captures the intended evaluation order.

This is the deepest reason the tree is called *abstract*: it abstracts away the syntactic mechanism (parentheses) and replaces it with the structural reality (depth/nesting).

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["BinaryExpression op=+"] --> B["BinaryExpression op=*"]
  A --> C["Literal value=5"]
  B --> D["Identifier name=x"]
  B --> E["Literal value=2"]
sections.caption: AST for `x * 2 + 5`. The `*` node is a child of the `+` node — meaning multiplication is evaluated first. Changing the source to `x * (2 + 5)` would flip the parent-child relationship.

sections.title: Tree Traversal: Depth-First and the Visitor Pattern
sections.content:
Having an AST is only useful if you can **walk it** — visit every node in a systematic order and do something at each node. The standard approach is **depth-first traversal**, which visits a node and then recursively visits all of its children before moving on to the node's siblings.

Depth-first traversal has two sub-variants:
- **Pre-order** (enter): process the node *before* its children. Used by most code analysis tools — you see a `FunctionDeclaration` before you see the expressions inside its body.
- **Post-order** (exit): process the node *after* its children. Useful for evaluation (you need operand values before you can compute the parent operation) and for bottom-up code generation.

Most real tools use **both entry and exit hooks** — enter a scope when you encounter a `BlockStatement`, exit the scope when you leave it. This is how ESLint tracks variable scopes.

The standard software pattern for this is the **Visitor pattern**. Instead of putting switch logic inside the traversal function, you provide a *visitor object* — a map from node type strings to handler functions. The traversal engine calls the right handler automatically:

```js
visitor = {
  BinaryExpression(node) { /* called for every BinaryExpression */ },
  Identifier: {
    enter(node, parent) { /* called when entering */ },
    exit(node, parent)  { /* called when leaving */ }
  }
}
```

The Visitor pattern has an important property: **traversal is decoupled from the operation**. The same `walk` engine can run a linting visitor, a type-checking visitor, and a code-generation visitor over the same AST, independently. You do not need to modify the traversal code to add new operations — you just write new visitors.

**Babel's traversal engine** calls each visitor with a **path** object, not just the raw node. A path wraps the node and provides a rich API: `path.replaceWith(newNode)`, `path.remove()`, `path.insertBefore(node)`, `path.skip()` (skip visiting children). This is what makes Babel transforms so expressive.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: We build three independent visitors over the same AST: a name collector, a tiny interpreter, and a lint rule. Each visitor is a plain object; the `walk` function calls the right handler for each node type. Notice how `evalNode` works post-order by nature — it recursively evaluates children before computing the parent — while the linting visitor is purely pre-order.

sections.title: Real AST Shapes: The ESTree Specification
sections.content:
In the JavaScript ecosystem, almost every tool agrees on the **ESTree specification** for AST node shapes. ESTree was originally derived from the SpiderMonkey (Firefox) parser's output and has become the de-facto standard. Babel uses a superset of ESTree (adding TypeScript and Flow-specific nodes). ESLint uses ESTree directly. `acorn` produces ESTree nodes.

Knowing the ESTree shapes by heart makes you immediately productive when writing plugins and rules. The most important patterns:

**Variable declarations.** `const x = 42` produces a `VariableDeclaration` with `kind: 'const'` and a `declarations` array containing a single `VariableDeclarator`. The declarator has `id: Identifier('x')` and `init: Literal(42)`. Note that `declarations` is always an array — `const a = 1, b = 2` is one `VariableDeclaration` with *two* declarators.

**Method calls.** `console.log('hi')` is a `CallExpression`. Its `callee` is a `MemberExpression` — `object: Identifier('console')`, `property: Identifier('log')`, `computed: false`. The `arguments` array contains `[Literal('hi')]`. This nested structure means a linting rule for `no-console` must check `callee.type === 'MemberExpression' && callee.object.name === 'console'`.

**Arrow functions.** `(x) => x * 2` is an `ArrowFunctionExpression`. If the body is a single expression (no braces), the `body` field holds that expression directly and `expression: true`. If the body uses braces, `body` is a `BlockStatement` and `expression: false`.

**Template literals.** `` `Hello ${name}!` `` is a `TemplateLiteral` with a `quasis` array (the string parts, as `TemplateElement` nodes) and an `expressions` array (the interpolated expressions). The quasis and expressions alternate: `['Hello ', '!']` and `[Identifier('name')]`.

**Spread and rest.** `...args` in a function call is a `SpreadElement`; in a function parameter it is a `RestElement`. Same source syntax, different node type depending on context — a nuance that trips up first-time plugin authors.

The fastest way to learn these shapes is **astexplorer.net** — paste any code snippet and instantly see the full parsed tree. It supports dozens of parsers and is the single most useful tool for AST work.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: These are the exact ESTree node shapes you will encounter in real Babel plugins and ESLint rules. The `no-console` rule checks `CallExpression` nodes and inspects the `callee.object.name`. A Babel plugin receives a path object with methods like `path.replaceWith()` — here we simulate the interface with a plain object to illustrate the shape without needing a real Babel install.

sections.title: How Tools Use the AST: Linters, Transpilers, Formatters
sections.content:
The AST is not an end in itself — it is the foundation that every major JS tool is built on. Understanding what each tool does at the AST level demystifies them completely.

**ESLint — static analysis via visitors.** ESLint parses your source to an ESTree AST, then runs each configured rule as a visitor over the tree. A rule like `no-unused-vars` uses scope analysis (built on top of AST traversal) to find `Identifier` nodes that are defined but never read. A rule like `prefer-const` finds `VariableDeclaration` nodes with `kind: 'let'` where the `VariableDeclarator.id` is never reassigned. Rules can report errors with precise positions because every AST node carries `start`/`end`/`loc` from the original source.

**Babel — AST-to-AST transformation.** Babel's pipeline is: parse → traverse with plugins → generate. Each plugin registers visitors. When the traversal engine visits a node that a plugin registered interest in, the plugin can mutate the AST in place — replacing the node with a different node, removing it, or inserting siblings. After all plugins run, Babel's code generator walks the final AST and prints it back to JavaScript source text. Crucially, Babel does not do string replacement. It transforms the *structure* and re-prints — which is why it can preserve formatting intent and generate source maps.

**Prettier — AST-aware pretty-printing.** Prettier is more radical: it completely ignores the original formatting of your source. It parses the code to an AST, then traverses the AST and rebuilds the formatted source from scratch, following its own opinion about line lengths, indentation, and bracket placement. The original source code's whitespace is irrelevant — Prettier only cares about the tree. This is why Prettier is truly idempotent: running it twice produces the same output, because the second run starts from the same AST structure.

**TypeScript — typed AST with two passes.** TypeScript adds a second tree layer: it parses source into an AST, then runs a **type checker** that annotates nodes with type information, building a **type-annotated AST** (sometimes called a symbol table). The `tsc` compiler then walks this annotated tree to check for type errors and emit JavaScript. TypeScript's compiler API exposes this annotated tree, which is why TypeScript-aware tools (like ts-morph) can do rich refactoring that understands types, not just syntax.

**Webpack / Rollup — module graph from AST.** Bundlers parse each module's AST and trace `import` and `require` statements to build a **module dependency graph**. They then walk this graph to determine which modules are needed, apply tree-shaking (removing `export`ed identifiers that are never imported anywhere), and concatenate the remaining code into a bundle. Tree-shaking is only possible because the bundler understands the AST: it can see which exports are referenced and which are dead code.

sections.title: Source Maps: Connecting Generated Code Back to the Original
sections.content:
When Babel transpiles TypeScript to JavaScript, or when Webpack bundles a thousand modules into one file, the output code looks nothing like the input. Line numbers shift, variable names get mangled, code from different files is interleaved. If a runtime error occurs on line 47 of `bundle.js`, which line in *your* source caused it?

**Source maps** solve this. A source map is a JSON file (or inline base64 comment) that records a mapping from every position in the generated output back to the corresponding position in the original source. The format encodes these mappings with VLQ (variable-length quantity) encoding to keep the file compact.

Browser developer tools automatically fetch source maps (when the `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment is present) and display the original source. You set breakpoints in your TypeScript, even though the browser is running compiled JavaScript — the devtools translate positions transparently using the source map.

Source maps are generated during the code generation phase — when a tool walks the AST and emits text. Since every AST node carries its `start`/`end`/`loc` from the original source, the generator knows exactly which part of the original text each output span corresponds to.

For production deployments, source maps are typically served separately (not embedded in the JS file itself) and may be restricted to authenticated error tracking services like Sentry, so end users cannot reverse-engineer your source.

sections.title: Writing a Babel Plugin from Scratch
ASTs Beyond JavaScript: Universal Application
sections.content:
Every language that has a compiler, interpreter, or sophisticated toolchain works with ASTs internally. The node types differ, but the concepts — tree of syntactic constructs, visitor-based traversal, source positions, transformations — are universal.

**Python.** The `ast` module in Python's standard library gives you full access to the AST of any Python source. `ast.parse(source)` returns the tree; `ast.walk(tree)` iterates all nodes; `ast.NodeTransformer` is the Visitor-pattern base class for writing transforms. Tools like `pylint`, `mypy`, `black`, and `pyflakes` are all built on this.

**HTML and CSS.** HTML is parsed to a **DOM tree** (Document Object Model) — literally an AST for HTML. CSS is parsed to a **CSSOM tree**. PostCSS parses CSS into its own AST, letting plugins transform CSS (autoprefixer, cssnano) the same way Babel transforms JS.

**SQL.** Tools like `sqlfluff` (linter) and `dbt` (transformation) parse SQL into ASTs to check syntax, reformat queries, and analyse joins. Query planners inside databases also maintain internal AST representations of queries before optimising them.

**Go.** The `go/ast` package provides the AST for Go source. `gofmt` (the Go formatter) and `go vet` (the linter) are built on it. The entire Go toolchain is designed around programmatic AST access.

The insight is that once you understand how an AST works in one language, you can transfer that understanding to any other language's tooling. The vocabulary changes; the pattern does not.

**A brief history of syntax trees.** The concept of the AST was formalised in the 1950s and 60s as compilers moved from single-pass to multi-pass designs. John Backus's work on FORTRAN (1957) produced one of the first real compilers, and the Backus-Naur Form notation he co-invented (for ALGOL 58) became the standard way to write grammars that parsers translate into trees. The term *abstract syntax tree* itself is commonly traced to the Lisp community, where the in-memory representation of Lisp code *is* the AST — Lisp's famous parenthesised syntax `(+ x (* 2 y))` is a direct textual rendering of a tree. This property — that code and data share the same structure — is called **homoiconicity** and is what makes Lisp macros so powerful: a macro is literally a function that transforms one AST into another.

**Common mistakes and interview insights.** When writing an ESLint rule or Babel plugin, the most frequent mistake is assuming a node type is more specific than it is. For example, `obj?.method()` is a `CallExpression` whose `callee` is a `MemberExpression` with `optional: true` — not a separate node type. Always check the shape on astexplorer.net before writing the condition.

In interviews, if asked how a linter like ESLint works, the correct answer is: it parses source to an AST using a parser (like espree), then runs each rule as a visitor function over the tree — not via string matching or regex. Regex on source code is fragile and cannot understand nesting; an AST visitor is precise.

Another common interview question: how does Prettier guarantee idempotency? Answer: it discards the original source text entirely and reprints the AST from scratch, so the second run parses the already-formatted output and produces the same AST — printing it again gives identical output.

items: An **AST** is a tree where each node is a syntactic construct (literal, operator, function, statement). The word *abstract* means surface syntax (parentheses, semicolons) is discarded — only structure that determines meaning is retained.
Source text flows through **lexing** (characters → tokens) then **parsing** (tokens → AST). Downstream tools — linters, transpilers, formatters, bundlers — all consume the AST, never the raw text.

**Operator precedence** is encoded in tree depth: a child node is evaluated before its parent. Deeper `*` nodes mean multiplication happens before the addition in their parent node — no parentheses needed in the tree.

**Tree traversal uses the Visitor pattern**: a map from node type strings to handler functions. The traversal engine calls the right handler for each node it encounters, decoupling the walk algorithm from the operation being performed.

**ESLint, Babel, Prettier, TypeScript, and Webpack** all work on the same AST foundation. ESLint runs visitor rules; Babel transforms nodes; Prettier reprints the whole tree; TypeScript annotates with type info; Webpack traces import edges.
**Source maps** link positions in generated/transformed output back to the original source, enabling debuggers to show original TypeScript or JSX even when the browser is running compiled JavaScript.

ASTs are universal across languages — Python's `ast` module, HTML's DOM, CSS post-processors, SQL parsers, and Go's `go/ast` all follow the same core pattern. Understanding ASTs in one language transfers immediately to all others.

quiz.question: What does the word 'Abstract' mean in Abstract Syntax Tree?
options: The tree is generated using abstract classes for every node type.
The tree omits surface syntax details like parentheses and semicolons, retaining only structure that determines meaning.
The tree is an approximation produced by fuzzy parsing and may contain errors.
The tree uses abstract data types so nodes cannot be modified after creation.
quiz.explanation: Abstract means the tree abstracts away concrete notation — parentheses, commas, semicolons — that carries no semantic weight. Operator precedence and grouping are captured by tree depth instead.

quiz.question: In the compiler pipeline, what is the correct order of stages before tools like ESLint or Babel receive the AST?
options: Parser → Lexer → AST
Lexer → AST → Parser
Lexer → Token stream → Parser → AST
Source → AST → Token stream → Parser
quiz.explanation: The pipeline is: source text → lexer (produces token stream) → parser (reads tokens and builds the AST). Downstream tools like ESLint and Babel then receive the finished AST.

quiz.question: For the expression `x * 2 + 5`, why is the multiplication node a child of the addition node in the AST?
options: Because `*` has lower precedence than `+`, so it is processed later.
Because child nodes are evaluated after parent nodes, encoding that addition comes first.
Because `*` has higher precedence, child nodes are evaluated before their parents, so multiplication runs first.
Because the parser encountered `*` after `+` in the token stream.
quiz.explanation: Higher-precedence operations become deeper subtrees because children are evaluated before parents. Multiplication binds tighter, so its node is a child (evaluated first) and the addition node is the parent (evaluated after).

quiz.question: Which design pattern do AST traversal engines like ESLint and Babel use to call the right handler for each node type?
options: Strategy pattern — swap algorithm at runtime
Observer pattern — nodes publish events to subscribers
Visitor pattern — a map of node-type strings to handler functions
Command pattern — each node encapsulates an operation
quiz.explanation: The Visitor pattern separates the traversal algorithm from the operations performed at each node. A visitor object maps node type strings to handler functions; the traversal engine calls the matching handler for every node it visits.

quiz.question: In ESTree (the JavaScript AST standard used by Babel and ESLint), what node type represents `console.log('hi')`?
options: FunctionCall with a callee field
CallExpression with a MemberExpression callee
Identifier with a name of 'console.log'
ExpressionStatement with a MethodCall body
quiz.explanation: A function call is a `CallExpression`. For `console.log('hi')`, the `callee` is a `MemberExpression` (object: Identifier('console'), property: Identifier('log')). There is no 'FunctionCall' or 'MethodCall' node type in ESTree.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between how Prettier and ESLint use the AST?
options: ESLint reads the AST; Prettier only works with token streams.
ESLint runs visitor rules to flag bad patterns; Prettier discards the original text and reprints the AST with its own style rules.
Prettier modifies the AST in place; ESLint creates a new AST for the fixed output.
ESLint uses Babel's AST; Prettier uses its own custom parse tree format.
quiz.explanation: ESLint traverses the AST with visitor rules to report violations. Prettier ignores original whitespace entirely, traverses the AST, and regenerates the source from scratch according to its style rules — guaranteeing idempotent output.

quiz.question: A Babel plugin receives a `path` object instead of a raw node. What does `path.replaceWith(newNode)` do?
options: It creates a copy of the current node with updated fields.
It swaps the current AST node for a new node during the traversal.
It moves the current node to a different position in the tree.
It schedules the replacement to happen after the full traversal completes.
quiz.explanation: path.replaceWith() replaces the current node in the AST with the provided new node. This is the core mutation primitive used by Babel plugins — for example, replacing an ArrowFunctionExpression node with a FunctionExpression node.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a source map generated by tools like Babel or Webpack?
options: It maps CSS class names to the DOM elements that use them.
It stores the AST in a compressed binary format for faster re-parsing.
It maps positions in the generated/bundled output back to positions in the original source files.
It maps function names to their ESTree node types for documentation generation.
quiz.explanation: Source maps link positions in the generated output (compiled JS, bundle) back to the corresponding positions in the original source (TypeScript, JSX). Browser devtools use source maps to show original files when debugging.

quiz.question: In ESTree, the `ArrowFunctionExpression` node has a boolean field `expression`. When is `expression: true`?
options: When the arrow function uses the `async` keyword.
When the arrow function body is a single expression (no braces), not a BlockStatement.
When the arrow function takes exactly one parameter.
When the arrow function is passed as an argument to another function.
quiz.explanation: expression: true means the body field contains an expression node directly (the concise body form: `(x) => x * 2`). When false, the body is a BlockStatement (the block body form: `(x) => { return x * 2; }`).

quiz.question: Which property of Lisp (its homoiconicity) makes it uniquely related to the concept of ASTs?
options: Lisp programs run faster because they skip the lexing phase.
Lisp source code and its in-memory data representation are the same tree structure — code is data.
Lisp was the first language to use binary trees for arithmetic expressions.
Lisp macros are implemented using string interpolation, not tree manipulation.
quiz.explanation: Homoiconicity means Lisp's source syntax `(+ x (* 2 y))` is a direct textual rendering of a tree (list of lists). The AST is the data structure. This is why Lisp macros are functions that take an AST and return a new AST — macro expansion IS AST transformation.
